title: Backend Trading System
summary: Receive trading requests through a simple API.
Persist reliable state as the source of truth.
Process background work asynchronously and safely.

sections.title: Understanding
points: Clarify the request lifecycle from acceptance to completion.
Identify durability, latency, throughput, and consistency requirements.
Define the states, inputs, outputs, and failure boundaries.
speakingNotes: I would first confirm what must be synchronous and what can happen later.
The important contract is the request state and how a caller observes it.
I would make the reliability and scale assumptions explicit before choosing components.

sections.title: Approach
points: Keep the synchronous API path small and predictable.
Persist durable state before starting background work.
Use explicit, idempotent state transitions so retries are safe.
speakingNotes: I would separate accepting a request from doing the long-running work.
The database becomes the source of truth before an event is published.
This keeps the first version easy to operate while leaving room to scale.

sections.title: Core Solution
points: Validate and authenticate requests at a stateless API boundary.
Store request state in PostgreSQL with an idempotency key.
Publish work through a transactional outbox after the write commits.
Let workers consume events, apply the side effect, and update status.
speakingNotes: The API acknowledges only after the initial state is durable.
The outbox closes the gap between a database commit and event publication.
Workers can retry safely because the request and transition are idempotent.
sections.visual:
flowchart LR
  Client --> API
  API --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
  API --> Outbox
  Outbox --> Worker
  Worker --> DB

sections.title: Verification
points: Test duplicate requests, duplicate events, and concurrent worker claims.
Verify retries, dead-letter handling, and recovery from partial failure.
Monitor queue lag, processing latency, error rate, and stuck states.
speakingNotes: I would start with the failure cases because they define whether retries are safe.
The key tests cover duplicate delivery, database failure, and worker restarts.
Operational signals should show both customer impact and where work is stuck.

sections.title: Wrap-up
points: Start with a small stateless API, one database, and one worker pool.
Scale API, queue consumers, and storage independently as demand grows.
Keep ownership of every state transition clear and auditable.
speakingNotes: The design optimises first for durable state and safe recovery.
I would add capacity and operational complexity only when measurements require it.
The same five-part structure can carry a coding, debugging, database, or analysis answer.
